chapter: Technique, jam sessions, audiences and records
title: Two repertories, but record men wanted only hot numbers
summary: The band kept Black and White repertoires, and recording men wanted only hot numbers, not waltzes, from colored bands.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: You raised a point. You were saying that the White functions used to prefer waltzes and that kind of thing.
And in fact, since most of the dance halls, as far as II can understand, that even the Blue Devils played were White rather than Black....
You must have played an awful lot of waltzes.
I mean, you couldn't have played that much Jazz.
No. We played quite a bit of Jazz. In fact, we
kept two different repertories -- Black ones and White.
What I wanted to know, then: Why was it that when bands like the Blue Devils recorded, they never recorded waltzes; they always recorded the Jazz and Blues numbers?

Well, that's what the recording man asked for. He wanted something that was hot. Yeah. He didn't want nothin' that didn't have no pep to it. He wanted something hot. He wanted the hottest number we had. They didn't expect no pretty sweet music and no waltzes out of a colored band. They wanted you to play all hot stuff. Yeah. Now, Blues was all right. If you had some Blues, somebody gonna sing it and they thought it might go...
